extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, including required factual findings (Graham factors), KSR principles, rationales supporting obviousness, analogous art tests, examiner obligations, and applicant rebuttal burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Content of Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining what prior art exists in the relevant field, including references from the same or different fields of endeavor that address related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must make explicit findings about the scope and content of the prior art relied upon; references from other fields may be relevant if they address related problems (see analogous art guidance). Assess references in their entirety, including portions that teach away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences Between Prior Art and Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying what distinguishes the claimed invention from existing prior art disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate the specific differences between the claimed subject matter and prior art teachings—conclusory statements are insufficient. Findings should address the whole claimed invention and be supported by reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the education, experience, and problem-solving capability of a hypothetical person ordinarily skilled in the relevant art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make factual findings about skill level based on factors such as typical education, training, and work experience in the field; these findings affect what would have been obvious to that person and must avoid hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations (Objective Evidence of Nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence that may rebut obviousness, including commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are factual evidence that can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness. Examiners must evaluate such evidence and consider its nexus to the claimed invention; applicants bear the burden to present and substantiate these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Framework — Rejection of Rigid TSM
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court rejected rigid application of the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test and established a flexible framework for obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness can be found where predictable results follow from combining familiar elements, familiar techniques are applied in foreseeable ways, a finite number of predictable solutions exist, or design/market forces motivate variations. Examiners should consider the creativity of a person of ordinary skill and avoid rigid formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable Combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining known elements using established methods yielding expected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining prior art elements produces predictable results, that combination can support an obviousness rejection. Examiner should explain why the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple Substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing one known element with another to achieve predictable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substitution of elements is proper to support obviousness when the substitute is known and would be expected to function in the same way; examiner must show expectation of predictable success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known Technique Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a recognized technique to similar devices in comparable ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a known technique in a similar context, with an expectation of improved or predictable performance, can support obviousness. Explain similarity of contexts and expectation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready-for-Improvement Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Using known techniques on devices already recognized as needing enhancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a device is identified in the art as ripe for improvement, applying routine techniques to address that need may be obvious. Examiners should identify the prior art recognition of the need and the routine nature of the applied solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious to Try (Finite Predictable Alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting from limited, identified, predictable alternatives with reasonable success expectations ('obvious to try').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only a finite number of predictable solutions exist and a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success, an obviousness finding is appropriate. Identify the limited options and explain predictability/expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-Field Variations (Design/Market Incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting solutions from one field to another when market forces or design considerations justify the transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market or design incentives can motivate adaptation across fields; explain why a skilled person would have looked across fields and why adaptation would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Teaching/Suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit or implicit motivation in references to modify or combine teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference (or combination of references) may provide direct or implicit suggestion to combine or modify teachings. Examiners should identify the motivating disclosure and avoid relying solely on hindsight-based reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must be 'analogous art' to support an obviousness rejection; two tests apply: (1) same field of endeavor, or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test 1: A reference is analogous if it is within the same general technological area, even if it addresses a different problem. Test 2: A reference from another field is analogous if it is reasonably pertinent to the inventor's problem such that a person addressing that problem would consult it. Note: No analogous art requirement applies for anticipation (35 U.S.C. 102) rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual Findings Required (Examiners' Burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must articulate explicit findings regarding prior art scope, differences, and skill level, supported by reasoned explanation—not conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prima facie case of obviousness requires articulated factual findings rooted in the Graham factors. Unsupported conclusory statements are improper; each factual assertion should be explained and supported by the cited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole Invention Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be evaluated as a complete system, not reduced to isolated 'gist' or 'thrust' elements; inherent properties disclosed in specifications count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dissecting claims into over-simplified fragments. Consider the claimed invention in its entirety; include inherent properties and features disclosed in the specification when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindsight Avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis must reflect knowledge available at the relevant time, not inventor insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the invention as a template for reconstructing obviousness. Frame the analysis from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill at the relevant date (pre-AIA: time of invention; AIA: before effective filing date) without using inventor's later-discovered success as a roadmap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Considered in Its Entirety
rubrics_metrics.description: References must be assessed in their entirety, including portions teaching away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider all teachings of a reference, both those that support and those that discourage the claimed approach. Mere disclosure of alternatives does not necessarily constitute teaching away—explain why portions teach away if asserting such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's Rebuttal Burden After Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiners establish a prima facie obviousness case with proper Graham findings, the burden shifts to applicants to demonstrate examiner factual errors or provide evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must rebut with substantive showings (e.g., pointing out factual errors, presenting secondary considerations, demonstrating unexpected results). Mere unsupported assertions that common knowledge is 'unsupported' are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill — Considered Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners consider problem types encountered in the art, existing solutions, rate of innovation, technology sophistication, and education levels of active practitioners when defining the level of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to characterize what would have been within the creative capacity of a skilled person. Findings should balance against hindsight bias and consider examiner technical expertise; articulate how each factor informs the skill-level conclusion.
